input: Sampling an effluent stream in a truly representative manner is a more involved undertaking than simply filling a bottle at an outlet, and there are several important considerations that need to be taken into account. Firstly, the location at which samples are taken matters a great deal: samples should ideally be drawn at a point where the stream is well mixed, downstream of the last inflow and of any junction at which a side stream enters, since a sample collected from a quiet corner or from a partially settled flow will essentially reflect the composition of that particular corner rather than the composition of the stream as a whole. Where the stream is stratified, the sampling point should be relocated, or the flow should be mixed beforehand, because sampling a stratified stream at a single depth will only return the layer present at that depth. Secondly, a single sample is generally built up from a number of increments that are collected across the whole period which the sample is intended to represent, with the increments spread out through the discharge rather than being clustered together at its beginning. Each individual increment is small in comparison with the stream, and the increments are combined into a single composite, ideally in proportion to the flow at the moment at which each increment was taken, so that a high-flow part of the period contributes more to the composite than a low-flow part. Finally, it is important to understand why a single grab sample can be so misleading. An effluent stream is not steady in its composition: it varies with the operations taking place upstream, with batches being discharged, washed down, or started up, and a grab sample essentially freezes a single moment of that variation and reports it as though it were the stream itself. It is worth noting that no numerical limits are quoted in this passage; the regulatory limits that apply to the stream belong to the site's permit, and the sampling approach needs to serve those limits rather than to restate them.
target: Representative sampling of an effluent stream rests on where the sample is taken, how the increments that form one sample are gathered, and how the increments are combined. The sampling point is placed where the stream is mixed, downstream of the last inflow and of any junction that adds a side stream, because a sample drawn from a quiet corner or from a partly settled flow carries the composition of that corner rather than of the stream. Where the stream is stratified, the point is moved or the flow is mixed first; sampling a stratified stream at one depth returns the layer at that depth. One sample is built from increments taken across the whole period the sample has to represent, at intervals spread through the discharge rather than clustered at its start. Each increment is small beside the stream, and the increments are combined into a single composite in proportion to the flow at the moment each was taken, so that a high-flow part of the period contributes more than a low-flow part. A single grab sample misleads because an effluent stream is not steady: its composition swings with the operations upstream, with batches discharged, washed down, or started up, and a grab sample freezes one moment of that swing and reports it as the stream. The grab sample is not wrong about its moment; it is wrong about the period. A composite built from spread increments averages the swing instead, and what it reports is the composition of the discharge as a whole, which is the quantity a comparison against the permit turns on. Numerical limits are not quoted here; the limits that govern the stream belong to the site's permit, and the sampling method has to serve those limits rather than restate them.
